passages.t: ‘From everlasting to everlasting You are God’
passages.happening:
Psalm 90 opens Book Four of the Psalms, and it is the only psalm with Moses' name over it. The heading reads, “A prayer of Moses the man of God” (verse 1).

It begins with home. “Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations” (verse 1). Before anything else existed, God was. “Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God” (verse 2).

Then the psalm sets us beside him, and we look very small. “You return man to dust, saying, ‘Return, O sons of mortals’” (verse 3). “For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night” (verse 4).

Human life is like grass. It “springs up new” in the morning, “but by evening it fades and withers” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘The man of God’ is what Deuteronomy calls Moses: “the blessing that Moses the man of God pronounced upon the Israelites before his death” (Deuteronomy 33:1). Readers hold different views about the heading, as the book page explains for all the headings. Many Jews and Christians through the centuries have taken the psalm as Moses' own prayer, and it fits his years in the wilderness, when a whole generation died in the desert (Numbers 14:29). Many modern scholars think it was written much later and set under Moses' name, at the start of Book Four, to answer the crisis of Psalm 89. Others take a middle view. The psalm's message does not depend on settling it.

The book page notes that Book Three ended with Psalm 89's cry over the fallen king. Book Four begins by going back before any king, to Moses, and before Moses, to God who was there ‘before the mountains were born’.

A ‘watch of the night’ was a few hours of guard duty on the city wall. To someone asleep it passes in a moment. That is how a thousand years look to God.

In the land of Israel, grass grows fast after rain and dries up fast when the hot wind blows. Everyone had seen it happen in a day.
passages.later:
The first words God spoke about death in the Bible are behind verse 3: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

Isaiah uses the same picture of grass: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Peter takes up verse 4: “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day” (2 Peter 3:8).
passages.asks:
Where is your home? Psalm 90 does not start with a place. It starts with a person: ‘Lord, You have been our dwelling place.’ Houses change, towns change, families move. God has been the home of his people through every generation.

When life feels short and fragile, start where the psalm starts, with the God who was there before the mountains, and is there still.

passages.happening:
Now the psalm grows heavier. Our short lives are lived under God's anger at sin. “For we are consumed by Your anger and terrified by Your wrath” (verse 7). “You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence” (verse 8). We “finish our years with a sigh” (verse 9).

Then comes the famous line about how long a life is. “The length of our days is seventy years” (verse 10), it says, “or eighty if we are strong”. Even then, life is full of “labor and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away” (verse 10).

The psalm ends this part with a prayer. “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Seventy or eighty years was not the usual lifespan in the ancient world. Many children died young, so the average was much lower. The psalm is speaking of a full, long life for those who lived it out. Even that, it says, is short. Verse 10 is not a rule that sets the length of every life. The Bible says Moses himself lived to 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7).

The psalm speaks plainly about death. It does not call it natural or friendly. It ties death to human sin and to God's judgment on it, as Genesis does. That is a hard word. But it is spoken inside a prayer, to the God who is our home.

‘Number our days’ does not mean counting them out of fear. It means learning that our days are few and precious, so that we use them well. A ‘heart of wisdom’ is a life that lives in the light of that truth.
passages.later:
James asks, “What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (James 4:14).

Jesus told a man who had built bigger barns, “This very night your life will be required of you” (Luke 12:20). He also said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies” (John 11:25).
passages.hard:
Psalm 90 names death plainly, and some readers come to it grieving. If you have lost someone, perhaps before their seventy years, this psalm does not say that God shortened their life as a punishment for their own sins. It speaks of the human race as a whole, living under the shadow of death since Genesis 3. No one may use verse 7 to tell a grieving family that their loss was deserved.

Paul wrote that Christians do grieve, but “not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief feels too heavy to carry, please tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Try verse 12 as a daily prayer: ‘Teach me to number my days.’ It is not morbid. People who know their days are few often learn what matters most. Ask yourself what you would do differently if you took that seriously this week.

And look at verse 8. ‘Our secret sins’ are in the light of God's presence. That could frighten us. It can also free us. There is nothing to hide from the one who already sees.

passages.happening:
The psalm turns to asking. “Return, O LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on Your servants” (verse 13).

Then a prayer for joy. “Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days” (verse 14). “Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us” (verse 15).

They pray for their children too. “May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children” (verse 16).

And the last line asks that a short life might still count. “May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands” (verse 17), it says, and then says it again: ‘yes, establish the work of our hands’.
passages.hearers:
‘Return, O LORD’ (verse 13) uses the same word as verse 3, where God tells people to ‘return’ to dust. Now the people ask God himself to turn back to them. It is close to what Moses prayed on Mount Sinai, after the golden calf: “Turn from Your fierce anger and relent from doing harm to Your people” (Exodus 32:12).

‘In the morning’ (verse 14) is a picture people would feel. After a long, hard night, morning light was relief. The prayer asks for God's loving devotion, his hesed, to meet them like morning.

The last verse asks something very human. Our lives are short. Will anything we do last? The psalm asks God to make our work hold. It does not ask for fame. It asks for God's favour, so that what our hands made is not wasted.
passages.later:
Lamentations says of the LORD's mercies, “They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23).

Paul gives the answer to verse 17 in the light of the resurrection: “Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).
passages.asks:
What is the work of your hands? A job, a home, children, a garden, a small kindness no one sees. Psalm 90 lets you ask God to make it last.

And let verse 14 shape your mornings. Before the day's work begins, ask God to satisfy you with his love. A short life that begins each day with him is not a wasted one.
